writing.label: Written by Peter Green — not Santana
trail: The song is credited to Peter Green, who wrote it for Fleetwood Mac — the band he founded — and recorded it first in 1968.
Santana’s 1970 version is so definitive that the song is widely assumed to be theirs. They made it famous; Green wrote it.
The same page’s other story is the recording (above): Fleetwood Mac released it first, and Santana’s is the cover that eclipsed it.

answer.label: Not a Santana original — a 1968 Fleetwood Mac song by Peter Green
answer.originalArtistDates: British blues band · formed 1967 by Peter Green
answer.sourceLine: The twist has two parts. Almost everyone takes ‘Black Magic Woman’ for a Santana original, but Santana’s 1970 version is a cover — and the band they covered is one most people would never guess. The song was written by Peter Green and first recorded by Fleetwood Mac in 1968, in the years when Fleetwood Mac was a British blues band led by Green, long before the Rumours-era pop group most listeners picture.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Blue Horizon
original.released: Released as a single on 29 March 1968 in the UK (Blue Horizon 57–3138), written and sung by Peter Green
original.charted: Reached No. 37 on the UK Singles Chart; did not chart in the US
original.writer: Peter Green (who also sang and played on the original)
original.cover: Santana — released November 1970 on the album Abraxas (Columbia), as a medley with Gábor Szabó’s ‘Gypsy Queen’. It reached No. 4 on the US Billboard Hot 100 and became one of Santana’s signature songs, far outstripping the original.
trail: The song was written by Peter Green and first recorded by Fleetwood Mac, released as a single in March 1968 on the Blue Horizon label Wikipedia ↗.

This was the original, blues-focused Fleetwood Mac that Green had founded in 1967 — a very different band from the pop group of Rumours. Green wrote, sang, and played guitar on the record, which reached No. 37 in the UK and made no impression in America.

Santana recorded their Latin-rock version for the 1970 album Abraxas, pairing it with Gábor Szabó’s ‘Gypsy Queen’. It reached No. 4 on the US pop chart and so thoroughly eclipsed the original that most listeners now assume it began with Santana SecondHandSongs ↗.

authors.name: Peter Green
authors.heading: About Peter Green
authors.bio: Peter Green (1946–2020) was the British blues guitarist who wrote ‘Black Magic Woman’ and recorded it first with Fleetwood Mac in 1968 — a band he had founded the year before. He was one of the finest blues players of his generation, admired by B.B. King among others, but struggled with mental illness and left the group in 1970. It is one of pop’s quieter ironies that the man who wrote a Santana staple is remembered, if at all, as a footnote to a band that became famous without him.

authors.name: Fleetwood Mac
authors.heading: About Fleetwood Mac
authors.bio: Fleetwood Mac recorded the original ‘Black Magic Woman’ in 1968, when they were a British blues band led by Peter Green — not the multi-platinum pop group of the Rumours era that most people picture. Only the rhythm section, Mick Fleetwood and John McVie, carried through to the later line-up. The gap between those two Fleetwood Macs is a large part of why the song’s origin is so widely missed.

authors.name: Santana
authors.heading: Why it gets pinned on Santana
authors.bio: Santana — the Latin-rock band led by guitarist Carlos Santana — released their cover of ‘Black Magic Woman’ on the 1970 album Abraxas, folding it into a medley with ‘Gypsy Queen’. Their version reached No. 4 in the US and became so identified with the band that the Fleetwood Mac original vanished from public memory. The record is genuinely theirs and genuinely great; the only error is assuming a 1970 Santana hit must be where the song began.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a double misattribution: nothing about Santana’s record is wrong or fake, but it is a cover — and the band it covers is not the Fleetwood Mac most people know. A 1970 cover mistaken for the source, and a blues band mistaken for a pop one.

items.why: Santana’s 1970 version is a cover. The song was written by Peter Green and recorded two years earlier, in 1968, by Fleetwood Mac the history ↗.
This was Peter Green’s blues band, not the Rumours pop group — a distinction most listeners never make, which is why even people who know the name miss the connection.

items.tag: neither the famous band nor Santana
items.why: Green wrote and first recorded the song, yet he is the least-remembered figure attached to it. Authorship and fame belong to different people here.

misattribution.truthLine: Written by Peter Green, first recorded by the blues-era Fleetwood Mac in 1968, and made famous — but not originated — by Santana in 1970 the record ↗.

context.heading: Why the cover ate the original
lead: A cover eclipses its original most completely when the original has nowhere to hide. Fleetwood Mac’s 1968 ‘Black Magic Woman’ was a modest UK hit that never charted in America at all, so when Santana’s version arrived in 1970 there was no famous first record occupying the public’s memory to displace.

The confusion is compounded by a second gap: the band that recorded the original barely resembles the Fleetwood Mac most people know. In 1968 it was Peter Green’s blues group; by the late 1970s it was a California pop juggernaut with an almost entirely different line-up. Even listeners who know the name rarely connect it to a Santana song.
detailsBody: Peter Green writes ‘Black Magic Woman’ for his blues band Fleetwood Mac.
Fleetwood Mac record it first and release it as a single (March 1968, Blue Horizon).
The original reaches UK No. 37 and does not chart in the US.
Santana cover it for the album Abraxas, in a medley with ‘Gypsy Queen’ (1970, Columbia).
Santana’s version reaches US No. 4 and becomes the definitive one; the 1968 original fades from public memory.
context.pull: Even people who know the name Fleetwood Mac rarely connect the blues band that wrote it to a Santana hit.
